findings.title: Cache key leaks across org/project combos insecurely and uses hash() non-deterministically across process restarts
findings.body: Using Python's built-in hash() on a tuple of project ids for cache keys is risky: hash() for tuples is stable within a process but PYTHONHASHSEED can randomize hashes for strings in other contexts; more importantly, hash collisions are possible, meaning two different project-id sets could map to the same cache key and return a stale/wrong upsampling decision for an unrelated project set, causing wrong query behavior (either applying or skipping upsampling incorrectly). Should use a stable encoding (e.g. a sorted comma-joined string) instead of hash().

findings.title: Cached boolean conflated with None causes cache to never be effectively used when eligibility is False
findings.body: cache.get(cache_key) returning None is used to detect cache miss, but the cached value is itself a boolean that is False when the project set is not eligible. Depending on the cache backend, False may be stored/retrieved fine distinct from None, but this pattern is fragile — if the cache backend ever returns None for a falsy stored boolean (e.g. after serialization quirks or if cache.get default differs), the eligibility check will silently recompute every time, negating the intended performance optimization. More importantly, this means ineligible results are cached as `False` for 60s causing stale negative decisions if the allowlist is updated during that window, which combined with no cache invalidation call ever being wired in (see invalidate_upsampling_cache, which doesn't appear to be called anywhere) means allowlist updates take up to 60s to take effect — acceptable per docstring, but worth flagging since the invalidation function is dead code since nothing calls it in this PR, making it misleading/complete only on paper.

findings.title: upsampled_count() aliasing to 'count' only works for simple yAxis=count(), breaks for multiple metrics or custom aliases
findings.body: transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling replaces 'count()' with the literal string 'upsampled_count() as count', hardcoding the alias. If query_columns contains multiple aggregates or if downstream code expects the original alias format matching 'count()' (not aliased), this can conflict with existing alias logic in the query builder, produce duplicate alias errors when count() appears multiple times (e.g. in top events with multiple yAxis entries), or silently break non-count-only queries since only exact-match 'count()' survives transformation while equations/other representations of count referencing it won't be transformed consistently with the renamed alias.

findings.title: New upsampled_count() function unconditionally reads sample_weight column which may not exist
findings.body: The new SnQLFunction 'upsampled_count' directly references Column('sample_weight') without any guard. This function is reachable any time a query column is transformed via transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling, which is gated only by the allowlist/dataset heuristics in error_upsampling.py — not by verification that the underlying table/dataset actually has a sample_weight column. If this function is invoked against a dataset/table without that column (e.g. due to a bug in the eligibility heuristic, or future reuse of this function elsewhere), the query will fail with a column-not-found error at Snuba, surfacing as a 500 to users rather than a graceful fallback.

findings.title: is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects called repeatedly per widget-split sub-query re-reading cache/options each time
findings.body: _get_event_stats calls is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects on every invocation (including the up to 4 sub-queries performed for dashboard widget split-detection: error_results, original_results, transaction_results, and retry on exception). Although there's a 60s cache, this still does Redis/cache round trips multiple times per single HTTP request and recomputes `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` each time without caching, undermining the stated 'performance optimization' goal in the comments and adding unnecessary latency per request compared to computing it once outside the closure.

findings.title: Broad except Exception silently swallows malformed error_sampling context
findings.body: _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling uses bare 'except Exception: pass' twice, which will silently swallow bugs such as AttributeError from malformed contexts (e.g. contexts.error_sampling being a non-dict) or ValueError from float conversion, making test setup failures silently produce no sample_rate instead of surfacing a clear error, potentially masking real bugs in tests that rely on this helper.

findings.title: Test asserts upsampled count of 10 without verifying client_sample_rate-to-weight calculation logic
findings.body: test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects asserts count == 10 for events stored with client_sample_rate=0.1, implicitly assuming sample_weight = 1/client_sample_rate = 10. However there is no test anywhere in this PR for the actual sample_weight calculation/ingestion pathway (e.g., in event processing or factories) that sets the sample_weight column from client_sample_rate; the factories.py change only sets 'sample_rate' on normalized_data, not 'sample_weight'. This leaves a gap: the test may pass only if some other untouched part of the pipeline computes sample_weight = 1/sample_rate, which isn't verified or documented in this PR, making the test's correctness assumption unverified for reviewers.
